The farm, structure and stone cracker counts, the diversions and the cut-off dates come from the Volta River Authority's own resettlement plan and addendum, published by the Bank. The lender and the implementing agency are therefore reporting on their own project and no independent account of this line's land acquisition was found. The completion report says that by 2011 all outstanding compensation had been fully settled, including for the stone crackers, and does not say how long any individual went unpaid, how many people were affected by the works that began before payment, or how many of the 410 condemned structures were lived in. The addendum's cover prints July 2010 in a shifted-glyph font that text extraction renders as nonsense, so its date is on the document and the catalogue date matches it, though the file name says April 2011. The 2004 plan is dated December 2004 in its own running header and February 2005 on its cover, and both are given. The addendum's table of affected houses does not add up: its district rows give 226, 16 and 1 in the column for the original number of affected people and its total row gives 43 for that column, while its columns for properties on the original line and properties affected by diversion, 292 and 118, do sum to the total of 410. The Independent Evaluation Group's review prints no date on its pages; the 7 May 2018 date is the Bank's catalogue field and is likewise unverified at document level. The same report records recurrent cash flow difficulties at the Communaute Electrique du Benin which delayed disbursement of money set aside to compensate people affected by the Ghana-Togo-Benin 330 kV line. That line sits under the second phase and a separate project number, its construction was financed by other lenders, and the report says the Benin component financed by this credit raised no social safeguard issue because it required no land acquisition or resettlement, so that finding is not carried here.

The Volta River Authority prepared an environmental management plan and put it in the bidding documents, and prepared a compensation and resettlement action plan dated December 2004 before implementation, later supplemented by an addendum covering the people the diversions affected. Under the plan, affected people were compensated at the Authority's valuation of crops, land and buildings, or, where they disagreed, at the figure set by an independent valuation the Authority paid for. The addendum states that the absence of title documents did not bar a claimant from payment once ownership could be ascertained and validated, that replacement cost was estimated with no depreciation deducted, and that household relocation expenses were factored in as a disturbance element. The Benin component triggered only the environmental assessment policy, because the works there were upgrades to control and communications hardware at existing substations and required no land acquisition or resettlement, which the report states at paragraph 44 (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 28 February 2018; Resettlement Action Plan Addendum).

companies.role: Says on its own website that SONABEL and GRIDCo mandated it to deliver, on a turnkey basis, the 225 kV overhead line linking Bolgatanga to Ouagadougou together with the 225/90/33/33/34.5 kV Zagtouli substation and the 90/33 kV Patte d'Oie substation, both in Ouagadougou, over a project period from October 2016 to January 2018, with the link operational from June 2018 and inaugurated on 5 October 2018. The Bank's completion report refers to a single jointly engaged transmission line contractor and a single owner's engineer and names neither (Eiffage Energie Systemes company page; Implementation Completion and Results Report, 30 July 2019).

cases.community: The project built a 225 kV transmission line between Bolgatanga in northern Ghana and Ouagadougou, 171 km of it from the Zagtouli substation to the border at Dakola and Paga and 17 km from the border to the Bolgatanga 2 substation, plus substations at both ends and shield-wire supplies to 11 villages along the route. The completion report records two fatal accidents in July 2017, less than a month apart. In the first, a transmission tower gave way while a team of two workers were carrying out assembly works on it; the tower fell to the ground carrying both men, one was declared dead at the scene and the other was seriously injured and admitted to hospital. In the second, a minor drowned in a pool that had formed in the excavated tower foundations after they filled with rain water. The report puts the accidents down to a supervision gap: only one health and safety supervisor was deployed by the owner's engineer for all the construction sites, which in places were hundreds of kilometres apart, and it says the need for more supervisors on projects covering a wide area became evident when the two deaths occurred. After the accidents the Bank's team worked with SONABEL, the owner's engineer and the contractor on a twenty-point action plan, which included certifying workers who install at heights, involving community organisations and non-governmental organisations in monitoring social activities, securing all work sites with wooden barricades before starting any work, applying the compensation provisions for such cases and producing evidence of the reports and of the start of compensation, and performing the sacrificial rituals the customary authorities demanded. Separately, the report records delays in paying compensation to project-affected people, which it attributes to some people presenting incomplete documents to back their claims, which took considerable time to verify and assess, and to farmers migrating to other places in Ghana by season so that they were not always available for the asset inventory surveys and the valuation. It says the Bank could not establish how effective the grievance redress mechanism was, because the issue only surfaced late in the project when a complaint about delayed compensation was escalated, and that there was no formal mechanism in place, only a default verbal process in which traditional and local government authorities acted as go-betweens. The resettlement action plan for the Ghana section, prepared before appraisal, counted 1,166 project-affected people in 87 households in the Bolgatanga Municipality and the Kassena-Nankana East and Kassena-Nankana West districts, giving an average household size of 13.0, of which 8 households were headed by women. The sentence that gives the 1,166 says the 87 households lie in all the 16 communities affected; elsewhere the same plan calls them fifteen settlements and says all the 15 communities have access to potable water. It recorded that of 150 owners of compounds and gates surveyed, 142 lived by farming, 8 were government employees and 3 fished, that 43 of those who farmed also did leather work or basketry and 17 also did petty trading, and that only 17 of the 87 households had electricity and none had its own water supply. That survey covered a route that was then largely abandoned: the project's first restructuring cut the line from 210 km, of which 39 km lay in Ghana, to 188 km, of which 17 km lay in Ghana, so the plan's 87 households were counted along more than twice the length of line finally built in Ghana. It also recorded that the corridor, 40 metres wide over the 39.3 km of line originally planned inside Ghana, would be cleared of all trees above about 1.25 metres and that if the corridor were not acquired and the affected people not resettled before clearing, the clearing would create conflict between the project promoters and the owners of the properties.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1,166 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The same figure appears in the resettlement action plan for the Ghana section as the population of the 87 affected households at the planning stage. No document found gives a count of people actually relocated, and the completion report gives no outcome figure for the resettlement at all.
cases.killed_note: Both counted deaths are in the completion report's health, safety, environment and social impacts section: a worker declared dead at the scene when a transmission tower gave way during assembly works, carrying two workers to the ground, and a minor who drowned in a pool formed in excavated tower foundations filled with rain water. The report attributes the pair to a supervision gap, says the need for more health and safety supervisors became evident when the two accidents occurred, and records in its lessons that if the measures later put in place had been implemented earlier the accidents might have been avoided. The Independent Evaluation Group's 2024 performance assessment states the cause as insufficient contractor implementation and enforcement of on-site safety measures. No other death is recorded in any of the three Bank documents.
cases.outcome: The line was energised and the project closed on 31 December 2018. The completion report says the project led to a significant reduction in heavy fuel oil imports in Burkina Faso. The Independent Evaluation Group's review says the Bank team was late in responding and only organised a mission after both fatal accidents had happened, that the Implementation Status and Results Reports rated overall safeguard compliance Satisfactory or Moderately Satisfactory throughout, which it says did not seem justified in 2017 when the two deaths occurred or in the later years when there was still no grievance mechanism, and that the reports appeared to lack candidness in assessing safeguard compliance. A formal grievance redress mechanism for the Ghana Grid Company was established only in 2018, the final year of implementation. The Independent Evaluation Group returned to the project in a performance assessment report of 30 October 2024, prepared after a mission that included site visits at Zagtouli, which states that contractor implementation and enforcement of on-site safety measures were insufficient, resulting in two fatalities and the serious injury of a third worker, that the project had no project-specific grievance redress mechanism until near the end of implementation and workers had no redress mechanism at all, and that the compensation delays on the Ghana side held up completion of the civil works by two months.

The 2024 report counts two fatalities and the serious injury of a third worker, where the completion report describes two workers on the tower, one killed and one seriously injured, and a minor drowned. No press report, court record, inquest or labour inspectorate finding on either death was found, in French or in English, and no document found names either person who died, says which contractor's site each accident happened on, or says where on the 188 km of line the accidents happened. The two Bank documents disagree on the dates: the completion report says both accidents occurred in July 2017, spaced less than a month from each other, while the review says the tower collapse was in July 2017 and the drowning a month later. The claim that all compensation was completed before closing is attributed by the review to the completion report's team rather than to a document. The identification of Eiffage Energie Systemes as the line contractor rests on the company's own account of its contract; the Bank's report names no contractor. cases.conditions: The project was environmental category B, partial assessment, and triggered four safeguard policies: environmental assessment, natural habitats, physical cultural resources and involuntary resettlement. Burkina Faso and Ghana each completed an environmental and social impact assessment with an environmental and social management plan, cleared by the Bank and disclosed in both countries and at the Bank in 2011, and each prepared and consulted on a resettlement action plan before appraisal. The Ghana-section plan annexes, and is built on, the Volta River Authority's own Land Acquisition and Resettlement Policy Framework of February 2007, prepared under the Ghana Energy Development and Access Project and stated to apply to all the Authority's land-based projects whatever their funding. Among that framework's principles were that before construction activities started the affected people were to be compensated, that affected people should be fully informed and consulted, that no impoverishment of affected people should result, and that compensation for loss of land, structures, crops and other assets was to be based on full replacement cost or market value, whichever was higher. Project appraisal concluded that both utilities had sufficient capacity to manage the potential negative impacts of the line and substation construction. The completion report records that this conclusion was wrong on health and safety supervision, that the Ghana Grid Company's grievance redress mechanism was not effective in recording complaints, and that no formal grievance mechanism existed until 2018 (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 30 July 2019; Volta River Authority Land Acquisition and Resettlement Policy Framework, February 2007).

cases.community: The project financed two 161 kV transmission lines in Benin, from Onigbolo to Parakou and from Sakete to Porto-Novo, together with substations and rural electrification. The appraisal document of May 2009 says these were the only parts of the project expected to have significant social impacts, and that the resettlement action plans found 123 families, about 640 people, needed to be physically resettled along the Onigbolo to Parakou route and 61 families, about 682 people, along the Sakete to Porto-Novo route; an annex to the same document puts the same two sets of figures as families who 'will need to be resettled and/or compensated'. The plans had first been prepared in 2004 and were updated in April and May 2008, and were disclosed on 21 January 2009 at the Bank and on 28 or 29 January 2009 in Benin. The completion report gives the outcome. It says most payments under the plan were made on time, that compensation for the first 50 km had been paid by October 2012, that plans were in place to begin the next phase in December 2014, and that a further 60 km of line was still unaccounted for. The Communaute Electrique du Benin assured the project team that all payments would be made by 31 December 2014 and had, in the report's words, 'encountered some resistance from those who had not received their payments'. The report then says it later became evident that the utility lacked the cash to make the payments as planned and had to seek a commercial short-term loan to cover them, and that the payments were eventually made in early 2015. Its account of what the delay did is blunter: the utility's lack of funds for the resettlement payments led to 'the to-be relocated people blocking progress on the line', and construction of the IDA-financed transmission line only began in 2016. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of the report puts the same sequence as the utility being expected to complete all payments by December 2014, failing to process them for lack of funds, and this resulting in protests from people who could not receive their compensation. In March 2018, during a supervision mission, the Bank found irregularities in the compensation of project-affected people for the transmission line and the electrification works, including 70 project-affected people who had been identified but did not show up. The client implemented an agreed action plan to close those cases, which included the utility setting aside the compensation amount for a determined period. The review puts the same finding as 70 people who did not receive their payments because they did not contact the utility. In December 2012 a Bank mission with a safeguards specialist rated safeguard implementation Moderately Satisfactory, noting that the arrangements for integrating the safeguard measures were not always followed and that studies, permits, certificates and monitoring reports were not disseminated or archived properly; semi-annual safeguard reporting only began in 2014.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1,249 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Bank's own planning figure is 184 families, about 1,322 people, across the two transmission lines: 123 families, about 640 people, on the Onigbolo to Parakou line and 61 families, about 682 people, on the Sakete to Porto-Novo line, from resettlement action plans first prepared in 2004 and updated in 2008. The appraisal document's main text says these families needed to be physically resettled; its annex says they would need to be resettled and/or compensated; the completion report repeats the 1,322 with the words 'resettled and/or compensated'; and the Independent Evaluation Group's review states it as 184 families consisting of 1,322 people who 'were to be resettled'. No document found gives a count of people actually relocated.
cases.suppression: No arrests, evictions by force or police action are recorded in the Bank's completion report or the Independent Evaluation Group's review. Both record action the other way: the report says people awaiting payment blocked progress on the line and that the utility encountered resistance from those who had not been paid, and the review calls this protests from people who could not receive their compensation.
cases.killed_note: No deaths are recorded in the completion report or the Independent Evaluation Group's review. The report records that the contractor's field workers were not paid for periods of up to six months while ownership changes were processed and went on strike.
cases.outcome: The project closed on 31 December 2018, three and a half years late, after the last extension was granted in part because compensation to displaced people was still pending. Compensation for the delayed stretch was paid in early 2015 and construction of the IDA-financed line began in 2016. The 70 people found uncompensated in March 2018 were dealt with under an action plan that set their money aside for a fixed period; neither Bank document says whether any of them was finally paid. The Independent Evaluation Group's review records that the project team confirmed the project was in compliance with the involuntary resettlement safeguard policy at closing.

cases.community: The project paid for new and upgraded grid stations, transmission lines and distribution networks across five state electricity companies. Resettlement action plans were prepared only by the companies that acquired land for grid stations, and an abbreviated plan by one more; in Lahore the Lahore Electric Supply Company acquired land from 15 affected people. The completion report says the major area of compensation was not the grid station land but crop and other losses suffered while the transmission line components were built. Those losses were handled under the companies' existing practice, which is to assess the damage after it has happened, through the patwaris or land revenue officers and local staff. The report states that in the absence of standardised guidelines and procedures for assessing losses, the common practice across all the distribution companies is to assess after the damage, that there is no clarity on the standardisation of compensation payments, and that 'the result was that compensation payments were severely and consistently delayed in the Project'. Three of the five companies, the Islamabad, Lahore and Multan companies, reported pending or outstanding payments even at the end of the project. In the case of the Islamabad company the payments were delayed for a year. The Multan company had paid 19 per cent of the compensation owed for crop losses by the end of the project. A grievance redress mechanism operated throughout, but the report says it had limited scope to address the main issue, the delays in assessing losses and awarding compensation for losses caused by the transmission lines. The project paid for social and environment cells inside each company to oversee social safeguards, but the report records that the project kept the existing system in which the land revenue officers and the sub-divisional officer concerned assessed compensation for transmission line work, that the cell was not part of that process and so could play no part in prompt assessment, in public consultation and outreach on the assessment, or in answering public grievances about it, and that this cut the cells' effectiveness. The report says compliance with safeguards was not satisfactory in the early years because the implementing agencies and their contractors lacked experience, and that it improved gradually.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1,303 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The only count of affected people in the Bank's own completion report is the 15 people whose land the Lahore Electric Supply Company acquired. The two companies' resettlement plans of 2006 count the people their transmission lines were expected to affect, as planning figures and not outcomes: the Islamabad company's plan gives 453 affectees along 286 km of temporary right of way covering about 2,145 acres, plus three landowners for four new grid stations, and the Multan company's plan gives 669 affectees on 1,339 acres of cultivated land across six transmission line components, with crop compensation estimated at Rs 9,626,145, plus four landowners for five new grid stations. No Bank document found gives a count of people actually relocated.
cases.killed_note: No death caused by the project is recorded in the completion report or the Independent Evaluation Group's review. The report's only fatality figures are a utility safety statistic it cites as a benefit: it says the installation of aerial bundled conductor in the Hyderabad company's network eliminated failure complaints and showed a drastic reduction in fatalities, with a footnote reading 'In FY13, HESCO reported zero public fatalities down from 18 and 11 in FY12 and FY11.' Those are counts of members of the public killed on that company's existing network before and during the works, not deaths caused by the project.
cases.outcome: The loan and credits closed on 28 February 2014 with compensation payments still pending at three of the five companies, and with the Multan company having paid 19 per cent of what it owed for crop losses. Only 66 per cent of the planned subprojects were completed by the revised closing date and 51 per cent of the planned cost was spent. The completion report rated the outcome Moderately Unsatisfactory and Bank performance Unsatisfactory; the Independent Evaluation Group agreed on both. The report's own lesson is that institutional reform on social safeguards, particularly on compensation payments, remains critical to the distribution companies functioning as modern, efficient entities embodying good practices on social issues.

cases.title: 239 People Unpaid When the Kampala Roads Credit Closed
cases.place: Kampala, Uganda
cases.point: Kampala. The works covered 26 roads, seven traffic junctions and drainage channels across the city's divisions, so one point cannot cover them (OpenStreetMap place point for Kampala)

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credit C4367 of US$33.6 million for the Kampala Institutional and Infrastructure Development Project (P078382), approved by the Board on 6 November 2007. Original closing was 31 December 2010; after two extensions totalling three years the project closed on 31 December 2013. Project costs were US$37.10 million at appraisal. A restructuring approved on 3 December 2010 extended the closing date by 24 months and created an additional category of eligible expenditure for involuntary resettlement, because the government could no longer fully finance the project's resettlement cost; a second restructuring on 27 December 2012 extended closing again from 31 December 2012 to 31 December 2013. Environmental category B. The implementing agency was Kampala City Council, which became the Kampala Capital City Authority during the project. The Independent Evaluation Group's review rated outcome Satisfactory and risk to development outcome Moderate and quotes the completion report by paragraph (IEG ICR Review ICRR14588, date posted 25 February 2015).

companies.name: Kampala City Council, later the Kampala Capital City Authority
companies.role: The city government of Kampala and the project's implementing agency; in 2011 the elected City Council was replaced by the Capital City Authority, a central-government body under a minister, with an Executive Director appointed by the president. The Independent Evaluation Group's review says a lack of capacity in the Council and Authority, compounded by insufficient government funding for the resettlement compensation, led to the compensation problems, and that the body had no specialist to handle safeguard issues (IEG ICR Review, 25 February 2015).

cases.community: The credit paid for rebuilding city roads, traffic junctions and drainage channels in Kampala together with reform of the city government. The resettlement action plan of October 2006 set out two design scenarios and recorded that under the second, which the City Council accepted for implementation, 415 entities, meaning individuals, households and businesses, were affected and 141 of them would relocate, some on the same plot and some to a wholly new site, with an extra 15 per cent on the value of the property allowed for the cost of moving. The plan's eligible categories ran from registered title holders down to licensees, those with the landowner's permission to put up a kiosk or grow seasonal crops but no legal claim, and squatters with neither legal nor customary claim. Its cut-off date was 15 April 2006. The plan set out a three-stage grievance procedure starting at the division office. Its table of the adopted scenario puts 91 of the 141 relocations on one work, the Lubigi primary channel, which runs through Kawaala; the rest are spread over five roads, four other drains and two traffic junctions. Its census counted 1,118 people in the corridor, 623 of them, 55 per cent, renting the premises for business, residence or both and 495, 45 per cent, claiming to own the property, and it put vulnerable households, those headed by women over 60, by very young women and by the unemployed, at 10 per cent. The Independent Evaluation Group's review gives the outcome: by the project's closing date of 31 December 2013, 494 project-affected persons had been compensated and 239 persons had yet to receive compensation. It attributes most of the outstanding payments, citing the completion report's paragraph 48, to unsubstantiated claims, and says that by the time the completion report was concluded all eligible claims had been paid off. On the environmental side it records deficiencies in safeguard implementation, especially at the landfill: poor handling of the landfill acquisition with no proper due diligence before the six-acre extension land was bought, incomplete fencing around the site, reliance on a temporary operating licence for longer than expected, and a leachate monitoring and treatment system not commensurate with the national waste water treatment and discharge standard, posing health and safety risks to the public. It says all of those were resolved within a month of the project closing.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1,118 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. That figure is in the project's own resettlement action plan of October 2006, to the person: the plan's census counted 1,118 people in the corridor, 623 renting and 495 claiming ownership. The project's own resettlement action plan of October 2006 counted 415 affected entities, meaning individuals, households and businesses, of whom 141 were to relocate under the design the City Council adopted. The Independent Evaluation Group's review counts 494 people compensated and 239 not compensated by the closing date, 733 in all. No document found gives a count of people actually relocated.
cases.killed_note: No deaths are recorded in the Independent Evaluation Group's review.
cases.outcome: The credit closed on 31 December 2013 with 239 people still unpaid. The Independent Evaluation Group's review says that by the time the completion report was concluded all eligible claims had been paid, attributing most of the outstanding payments to unsubstantiated claims, and rated the project's outcome Satisfactory. The Bank went on to lend for a Second Kampala Institutional and Infrastructure Development Project, approved 20 March 2014, under which an Inspection Panel case was later registered over the Lubigi drainage channel at Kawaala, the work that carried 91 of the 141 relocations planned under this first credit.

cases.confidence_note: The project's own completion report is not disclosed. Searches of the Bank's document archive under this project number, by title and by project name returned no completion report, so the figures of 494 compensated and 239 unpaid rest entirely on the Independent Evaluation Group's review of that report, which cites it by paragraph. The lender is therefore reporting on its own project at one remove, and the underlying document cannot be checked. Searches for Ugandan press or non-governmental reports on compensation under this first Kampala project found only material about its successor, the second project approved in 2014. No document found names any of the 239 people, says how long they waited, says which roads they were on, or says how many of them were among the 141 who were to relocate. The review says that by the time the completion report was concluded all eligible claims had been paid off and rated the project's outcome Satisfactory. The 415 affected entities and 141 relocations are planning figures from the October 2006 plan, not outcomes.
cases.conditions: The project was environmental category B, which triggered the Bank's policies on environmental assessment and natural habitats, and the policy on involuntary resettlement was also triggered. An environmental analysis with an environmental management plan was prepared at preparation stage, and a detailed resettlement action plan dated October 2006. The plan valued land and permanent structures at market value, which it says is higher than replacement cost in the city, and used the Council's 2003 rates for temporary and semi-permanent structures and crops. The Independent Evaluation Group's review says the Council and Authority had limited capacity and lacked a specialist to handle safeguard issues. Because the government could no longer fully finance the resettlement cost, the restructuring approved on 3 December 2010 created a new category of eligible expenditure under the credit for involuntary resettlement (IEG ICR Review, 25 February 2015; Resettlement Action Plan, October 2006).

cases.title: Compensation Nine Months Late in Tanzania's Strategic Cities
cases.place: Mbeya, Arusha, Ilemela, Mwanza, Kigoma-Ujiji, Dodoma, Tanga and Mtwara, Tanzania
cases.point: Mbeya, one of the cities where the completion report records land acquisition for a sanitary landfill buffer zone held up for want of counterpart funds, and where the project's March 2010 resettlement plan counted 35 affected buildings including fences, 6 areas with crops and 41 people to be affected by the city roads subproject. The project covered eight local government areas and one point cannot cover them (OpenStreetMap place point for Mbeya)

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credits IDA-47270 of US$163 million, IDA-54600 of US$50 million and IDA-59470 of US$130 million for the Tanzania Strategic Cities Project (P111153), SDR 236.2 million in all, about US$343 million. Approved 27 May 2010, effective 8 September 2010, mid-term review 8 May 2017. Original closing was 31 December 2015; actual closing was 26 November 2020, with a restructuring on 4 May 2020 extending the closing date. US$340,372,832 was disbursed of US$342,997,608 revised. Denmark was listed at approval as providing US$12.5 million and the completion report's financing table records nil for it at completion. There was no borrower contribution. The implementing agency was the Prime Minister's Office - Regional Administration and Local Government, renamed the President's Office - Regional Administration and Local Government during the project, working through the local government authorities of the participating cities. The completion report of 13 May 2021 rated outcome Satisfactory, Bank performance Satisfactory and monitoring and evaluation quality Substantial; the Independent Evaluation Group's review also rated outcome Satisfactory (Implementation Completion and Results Report ICR00005449, 13 May 2021; IEG ICR Review, Bank document date 22 October 2021).

companies.name: President's Office - Regional Administration and Local Government (PO-RALG)
companies.role: The arm of the Tanzanian presidency that supervises regional administrations and local government authorities, and the project's implementing agency. It reviewed and monitored the resettlement action plans the local authorities prepared, wrote the project's grievance redress manual and trained the grievance handling committees (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 13 May 2021).

cases.community: The project rebuilt roads, drains, bus stands, markets and landfills in eight Tanzanian local government areas. Each subproject had its own resettlement action plan, and the plans of March 2010 count what was to be taken. In Mbeya, the census for the city roads subproject found that the assets mostly affected were 35 buildings including fences and six areas with crops, and that 41 people would be affected; the plan's entitlement table says people without formal legal rights to the land are to be paid full replacement cost for their assets but nothing for land, because they are encroachers along the road reserve. In Arusha, 279 households were to be affected by the proposed upgrading works, 136 of them owning structures and land except for 42 households at the Murriet dumpsite who were entitled to compensation for structures only, 248 owning crops at four locations, 20 households owning land only, and 13 administrators acting for 23 deceased and a shrine; at Urundini two households were to lose their houses and a third his incomplete house, and at the Murriet dumpsite four households owned eight commercial structures and two of the residential houses to be removed were traditional thatched msonge houses. The Arusha plan records that corridors of 16 or 25 metres were contemplated, that a 16-metre corridor was proposed where the houses affected were concentrated, that even at 16 metres a number of houses would have to be partially demolished, and that owners of partly affected houses were concerned about their fate and felt they would be treated in future as encroachers in the road reserve if they were not resettled, a matter the plan says ought to be addressed at the second round of consultations. The Dodoma plan says about 29 households at Kikuyu and 21 at Chidaya village would have houses or other property affected, which at the plan's own average of 4.3 people a household it turns into about 100 people affected by the upgrading of the Kisasa community roads, and that among the affected structures are dwelling houses and several graveyards. It says 3 buildings and 20 farmlands were to be compensated at the Chidaya landfill site. It records that there were no resettlement issues on the Kisasa community roads because the people living along them had been required to leave the right of way since 2002, years before this project began, but that to conform to the Bank's guidelines those who had stayed on would qualify for a token relief; all of them had been given plots for relocation close to their original plots, and the city development authority had agreed to pay each household Tshs 400,000, made up of Tshs 300,000 for accommodation and Tshs 100,000 for transport. The completion report gives the outcome. It says the subprojects complied with the resettlement action plans but faced challenges because the local government authorities fell short in paying compensation and because designs changed, and that 'RAP implementation was often delayed sometimes to over nine months when LGAs lacked funds for compensation of PAPs thus delaying construction activities and raising complaints by PAPs.' It says another problem arose when subproject designs changed, especially on drainage, which changed who was affected, and that remedial actions were identified in the resettlement plan completion reports. Separately it records that insufficient counterpart funding from the local authorities was an ongoing issue through the life of the project, and that acquiring land for the sanitary landfill buffer zones in Mwanza, Kigoma-Ujiji and Mbeya and the road corridor wayleaves for Ilemela and Arusha all had periods when implementation was delayed for want of counterpart funds, despite repeated engagement between the Bank, the local authorities, the President's Office and the Treasury. It adds that delay in utility removal and compensation was revealed to be a source of grievances. Grievance handling committees were set up in all subproject areas and kept logbooks, but the report says the project included no grievance procedure at contractor level, which could have helped resolve and monitor complaints by workers, and that the grievance mechanism as a whole was characterised by a lack of funds because its activities were never budgeted at project design, leaving the committees' survival after closing uncertain.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1,054 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The project's own subproject resettlement plans of March 2010 count planned impacts city by city: 279 households in Arusha, 41 people in Mbeya, and about 29 households at Kikuyu and 21 at Chidaya village in Dodoma, where 3 buildings and 20 farmlands were to be compensated at the landfill site. The completion report gives no count of affected or relocated people at all, so there is no Bank outcome figure to set against ICIJ's.
cases.killed_note: No deaths are recorded in the completion report or the Independent Evaluation Group's review. The report notes that the project had no grievance procedure at contractor level, which could have helped document and monitor complaints by workers.
cases.outcome: The credits closed on 26 November 2020 and the completion report rated the outcome Satisfactory, as did the Independent Evaluation Group's review. The report records that payments to contractors were also often delayed for the same shortage of counterpart funds, which delayed contract execution and brought periodic complaints to the Bank from contractors. It says the delayed availability of counterpart funds is a portfolio-wide issue affecting other Bank-financed urban projects as well. Whether the people whose compensation was more than nine months late were eventually paid in full is not stated.

cases.confidence_note: This is the thinnest of the eight entries from this batch. The harm is a delay: the completion report says resettlement plan implementation was often delayed, sometimes to over nine months, when local authorities lacked funds to compensate affected people, and that this delayed construction and raised complaints. It attaches no count of people to that delay, does not say which cities the nine months applied to, does not say how many complaints were made, and does not say whether anyone went unpaid at closing. All the counts of people and structures given above are planning figures from subproject resettlement plans of March 2010, not outcomes, and the completion report publishes no outcome figure for resettlement at all. The report and the Independent Evaluation Group's review both rated the project Satisfactory and the report says the subprojects complied with the resettlement plans. The lender is reporting on its own project and no independent account of compensation under this project was found. The project has eight city resettlement plans and a later valuation volume; the counts above come from three of them, Mbeya, Arusha and Dodoma. The Independent Evaluation Group's review prints no date on its pages; the 22 October 2021 date is the Bank's catalogue field for the document and is unverified at document level.
cases.conditions: The project was environmental category B, partial assessment, and triggered three of the Bank's policies: environmental assessment, involuntary resettlement and physical cultural resources, the last of which matters because the plans count graves, a shrine and several graveyards among the assets affected. Environmental and social impact assessments, environmental and social management plans and resettlement action plans were prepared for the prioritised subprojects in each local government area, under an environmental and social management framework and a resettlement policy framework, using funds from an earlier Bank project to pay the consulting firms. The appraisal document records that draft assessments and plans for each city were disclosed at the Bank on 2 February 2010 and in Tanzania on 5 February 2010, and the final versions at both on 5 May 2010. Affected people were identified and compensation amounts set in line with Tanzanian law and the Bank's resettlement policy, and the plans were reviewed and monitored by the President's Office and the Bank. Paying the compensation was the local government authorities' own responsibility, as counterpart funding, and the completion report records that they repeatedly lacked the money. Grievance handling committees were set up in every subproject area, trained on a manual the President's Office wrote, and kept logbooks of complaints; the report says their activities were never budgeted at design, that there was no grievance procedure at contractor level for workers, and that their functioning after the project closed was uncertain (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 13 May 2021).

cases.title: Cracked Houses and Lost Grazing at Agarebi on the E60 Agara Section
cases.place: Agarebi village and the Agara bypass to Gomi bypass (Zemo Osiauri) section of the E60, km 114 to km 126, Kareli and Khashuri municipalities, Shida Kartli, Georgia

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA and IBRD)
lenders.role: Credit IDA-52450 of SDR 24.5 million, US$37.0 million equivalent, and loan IBRD-82630 of US$38.0 million for the Fourth East West Highway Improvement Project (P130413). Approved 9 May 2013, effective 5 August 2013, mid-term review 20 April 2016. The IBRD loan was reduced to US$35,023,065; US$35,738,583 of the credit and US$35,023,065 of the loan were disbursed, US$70,761,648 in all, against an original US$75 million. Georgia contributed US$21,549,436 against US$18,750,000 planned. Original closing was 28 February 2018; actual closing was 31 December 2019 after two restructurings, on 7 December 2017 and 27 February 2019, both extending the closing date. The implementing agency was the Roads Department of the Ministry of Regional Development and Infrastructure of Georgia. The Bank's policy on involuntary resettlement, OP 4.12, was triggered because the works on the 12 km from Agara to Zemo Osiauri 'required land acquisition causing both physical and economic displacement'. The completion report rated outcome Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory and monitoring and evaluation Substantial; the Independent Evaluation Group's review ICRR0022356 rated outcome Moderately Satisfactory and overall Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory (Implementation Completion and Results Report ICR00005191; IEG ICR Review ICRR0022356).

companies.name: COPRI
companies.role: Key contractor on the civil works contract for the Agara to Zemo Osiauri section (Implementation Completion and Results Report, P130413).

companies.name: Blacksea Group
companies.role: Georgian company engaged as sub-contractor to COPRI on the key civil works contract. The completion report describes it as one of the largest construction firms in Georgia and treats its engagement as an unintended benefit of the project (Implementation Completion and Results Report, P130413).

cases.community: The project upgraded 12 km of the E60 between the Agara bypass and the Gomi bypass at Zemo Osiauri. It acquired about 110 hectares in 571 land parcels, 40 per cent of it private land. The completion report records that 1,162 people in 272 households were affected, that five households were resettled, that four businesses stopped operating, that one construction material processing plant and 20 reservoirs were relocated within the company's own grounds, and that 20 ancillary and 45 minor structures were affected. GEL 8.2 million was paid for loss of land and crops, loss of buildings and structures, and livelihood restoration. The same paragraph records that no complaints related to land acquisition and resettlement were reported, and that the design of the second interchange was modified several times to reduce the resettlement impact. The resettlement process was completed in February 2018. The project's resettlement action plan of March 2017 gives the detail behind the five households. Thirteen residential houses were originally to be affected; a 2014 design change took all thirteen outside the resettlement corridor; the 2016 design update brought six residential houses owned by four households back under impact, and added two households with 11 affected people who had to be physically resettled, both at the second interchange. Of those two, the plan records that for one 'it was impossible to continue living in the house', and that the second 'was severally impacted as the house was damaged by construction works (the house started to get cracks, entry to the house will be blocked), hence the RD decided to relocate this AH'. The same plan lists the two operating commercial buildings lost as a boutique hotel, shop and storehouse complex and a gas filling station complex with an administrative building, boiler building, gas cylinder reception and workshops, watch building, transformer building and pumping station; their owners received one year of income compensation and replacement cost for the structures. A January 2018 addendum added one more household that was physically displaced, out of two households with seven members newly affected. Residents of Agarebi village, in the area of the second interchange, filed some 50 complaints about indirect damage from the highway works, mostly verbally, to the Roads Department and the contractor. The completion report says the Agarebi case 'took exceptionally long time to be resolved' and appears in mission reports from May 2017 onwards. Most complaints were settled quickly, with the contractor asphalting a local road, building an access road to the bus station, clearing a clogged irrigation channel and replacing damaged fences at its own expense. The complaints that took long were those about 'alleged damages (cracks) on several houses and loss of grazing land (due to loss of access) which led to reduction and eventually loss of cattle for a number of affected households'. A livelihood restoration plan giving money to the affected households was agreed with 44 of them and approved only in June 2020, six months after the loan closed.
cases.displaced_label: five households resettled, out of 1,162 people in 272 households recorded as affected (World Bank completion report, paragraph 68, P130413); the same count of five stands in the final column of the project's resettlement plan addendum of 11 January 2018, a month before the report records resettlement as complete
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1,011 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The completion report's own affected figure is higher, 1,162 people in 272 households, and its count of people actually resettled is five households. That table of 272 households, 1,162 people and five resettled households is also printed in the project's own resettlement plan addendum of 11 January 2018, under the heading 'Final updated 2018'; the completion report's verb is past tense and it records the resettlement process as complete in February 2018.
cases.outcome: The credit and loan closed on 31 December 2019. Resettlement was recorded as complete in February 2018, but the livelihood restoration plan for the 44 households at Agarebi whose houses cracked and whose cattle were lost was approved only in June 2020. The completion report rated the project's outcome Satisfactory; the Independent Evaluation Group rated it Moderately Satisfactory. The project also paid for feasibility studies and detailed designs for road sections to be built by other financiers, and the completion report records that this arrangement 'takes control over the quality of design documentation away from the Bank-financed project while attribution to EWHIP-4 remains'. A private agro-producing company complained to the Bank about inadequate information and consultation on pollution from construction and operation on one of those other corridors, where the environmental and social assessment had been financed by the European Investment Bank.

cases.confidence_note: Everything here comes from the Bank's own completion report, the Independent Evaluation Group's review of it, and the project's own resettlement action plan and its addendum, which the Roads Department of Georgia prepared. The lender is reporting on its own project and no independent account of the Agarebi village complaints was found. The completion report describes the complaints as 'mainly verbal', calls the cracks on houses 'alleged', and records that no complaints about land acquisition and resettlement were reported at all. No document found names any affected household, says how many cattle were lost, gives the amount of the June 2020 livelihood restoration payments, or says how long the Agarebi complaints went unresolved beyond the May 2017 starting point. The completion report's cover carries the date 30 September 2020. The Independent Evaluation Group's review prints no date anywhere on its 22 pages; 26 June 2021 is the Bank document date.
cases.conditions: The project was prepared under the Bank's safeguard policies on environmental assessment and involuntary resettlement. A resettlement policy framework was disclosed in February 2012 and a resettlement action plan in March 2013, with a replacement plan for the Agara to Zemo Osiauri section in March 2017 and an addendum in January 2018. The Borrower carried out a full-scale environmental impact assessment of the upgrading. The 'future studies' component financed feasibility studies and designs for road investments by financiers other than the World Bank but did not include the environmental impact assessments those designs needed, and the completion report records that the timing and quality of those assessments 'depended on external factors and interfered with the delivery of design documents'. Resettlement policy frameworks for the Jinvali-Larsi and Kvesheti-Kobi roads and for the Rustavi-Red Bridge and Algeti-Sadakhlo roads were prepared and disclosed under this project number in 2018 for works later financed by others (Implementation Completion and Results Report, P130413).

cases.place: Villages of Maes, Inkiene and Camp Yayé in the Manguenguengue and Monaco quarters of Maluku commune, Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Grant IDA-H8600 of SDR 72.9 million, US$110 million equivalent, for the Western Growth Poles Project (P124720). Approved 11 June 2013, effective 16 October 2013, mid-term review 15 May 2017. The revised amount was US$109,644,887 and US$101,498,675 was disbursed. Original closing was 30 August 2019; actual closing was 30 October 2020 after four restructurings, on 9 September 2015, 29 January 2018, 30 July 2019 and 27 April 2020. The Maluku special economic zone was component 2, allocated US$27 million at approval; the Independent Evaluation Group's review gives the actual figure as 'US$6', with no unit, where it gives millions for the other components. This was a category A project triggering seven safeguard policies, including involuntary resettlement. On 13 January 2016 the Bank notified the Government that it was partially suspending disbursements under category 2.3, the physical infrastructure for the zone, for 'poor implementation of the RAP for the SEZ of Maluku and the absence of an ESMP linked to the construction by the government of a wholesale market within the zone'; the suspension was lifted on 29 March 2017, 14.5 months later. The implementing agency was the Cellule d'Exécution des Financements en faveur des États Fragiles, the unit inside the Ministry of Finance that manages Bank-financed operations in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The completion report of 30 June 2021 rated outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory and monitoring and evaluation Modest; the Independent Evaluation Group's review ICRR0022662 agreed on outcome and Bank performance (Implementation Completion and Results Report ICR00005497, 30 June 2021; IEG ICR Review ICRR0022662).

lenders.name: International Finance Corporation
lenders.role: Ran the special economic zone programme that preceded the credit, set up at the request of the Democratic Republic of the Congo's Ministry of Industry in 2008 and ended in 2012. It identified the site and delivered the master plan, the environmental and social impact assessment and the resettlement action plan for the zone. It re-engaged after the public-private partnership was signed in January 2020 to structure advisory work towards an IFC investment (Implementation Completion and Results Report, annex 8, 30 June 2021).

companies.name: MIK
companies.role: Joint venture between the Government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the South African operator Africom. The completion report records that MIK 'had already launched physical works in the SEZ for the construction of ancillary infrastructure (access road, power supply and port), although safeguards requirements had not been adhered to, particularly the RAP that was being implemented and the requirement for MIK to conduct an environmental and social screening of the site, followed by a PGES'. The works were launched under the leadership of the Prime Minister's office in charge of agro-industrial development. The Bank's implementation report of 10 April 2016 records that the market was built on a 14-hectare plot the Government allocated inside the zone while the owner of that land had not been compensated, and lifting the Bank's suspension required, among other things, that this owner be compensated (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 30 June 2021).

companies.name: Strategos
companies.role: International private developer with which a public-private partnership for the zone was signed officially on 28 January 2020 (Implementation Completion and Results Report, annex 8, 30 June 2021).

companies.name: Artelia
companies.role: Consultants who carried out the field census of property, the geo-referencing of dwellings and the household survey behind the 2012 resettlement action plan for the zone (Plan d'Action de Réinstallation pour la ZES de Maluku, 27 August 2012).

cases.community: The project financed basic infrastructure for a special economic zone at Maluku, at the eastern edge of Kinshasa on the Congo river. The resettlement action plan of 27 August 2012, based on an Artelia field census with a 25 July 2012 cut-off, found 58 households losing a main dwelling and 37 further rightsholders losing buildings other than main dwellings covering 2,800 square metres, losing crops, or both. The plan did not count the people in those 58 households: it surveyed 46 of them, found 431 people, an average of 9.4 a household, and applied that average to all 58 to reach 'about 545 persons to resettle', of whom it puts 302 at children. It lists the 58 households one by one by village, street and household size, with households of 24, 20, 19, 17 and 15 people among them; its table numbers 21 of them at Inkiene and 37 at Maes, while its text says 22 at Inkiene and 37 at Maes. The losses also covered 39 hectares of farms and about 20 hectares of extensive cultivation and a football pitch; a cemetery was preserved. The zone's footprint was 233 hectares, of which 11.3 hectares were inhabited. Against that plan, the completion report records that the joint venture MIK started building the access road, the power supply and the port before the resettlement plan had been carried out and before the required environmental and social screening, and that the Government separately built a wholesale market inside the zone with no environmental and social management plan. The Bank's implementation report of 10 April 2016 is more specific about what the Bank objected to: the market was built 'on a plot of 14ha allocated by the Government within the Maluku SEZ while the owner of the land has not yet been compensated'. The Bank partially suspended disbursements on the zone's infrastructure from 13 January 2016 to 29 March 2017, and the completion report gives the ground for the suspension as non-adherence to the Bank's safeguard standards 'with regard to resettlements and compensation of owners being displaced because of the establishment of the SEZ'. Compensating the owner of the land the market stood on was one of the two conditions for lifting it. The report then gives the payments: 'The PDPC, with funds from the Government, executed the payment of 622 people listed in the project area for a total amount of US$ 4,422,055.68', of which US$3,906,544.01 was for the Maluku resettlement plan. In September 2018, 49 complaints from vegetable growers who had been working inside the pilot zone were submitted to the project; the report says that after the cases were handled, 37 people were declared eligible for compensation and received it, and says nothing about the other 12. The complaints the project logged were mostly about restricted access to resources or lost revenue, resettlement of populations and compensation, and disputes over who owned a particular asset. In one of them, compensation under a resettlement plan for an electricity line was paid to a man and an accomplice who were not the owners, to the detriment of the rightful owner of the neighbouring concession at the Lunga Vasa substation; that complaint was closed in December 2018 after negotiations between the parties. The report rates environmental and social safeguards overall moderately satisfactory, and records that supervision missions found the safeguard instruments were being adhered to.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 976 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The project's own resettlement action plan of 27 August 2012 plans for 58 households losing a main dwelling; its figure of about 545 people is not a count but the plan's own extrapolation, 431 people in the 46 households it surveyed applied across all 58. The completion report's only outcome figure is the 622 people paid US$4,422,055.68 with government funds, which it describes as people 'listed in the project area' and does not break down between those who were moved and those who lost land, crops or buildings. cases.killed_note: The completion report records that the Borrower reported around ten occupational health and safety incidents across the project's sites, most of them minor injuries to fingers or feet, and that no deaths were reported by the project unit during the whole project. cases.outcome: The grant closed on 30 October 2020. The Bank's suspension was lifted on 29 March 2017 once the owner of the land had been compensated and an environmental and social management plan had been prepared and cleared. Of the US$27 million allocated to the zone at approval, the Independent Evaluation Group's review records the actual figure as 'US$6', printing no unit where it gives millions for the project's other components. The basic infrastructure and a 6,155-metre protective wall were built with project funds, a national special economic zone agency was set up, and a public-private partnership with the developer Strategos was signed on 28 January 2020. The completion report's own annex presents the zone as a 'Success story' and makes no mention of the resettlement, the suspension or the growers' complaints; it also gives the zone's area as 244 hectares where the resettlement plan gives the footprint as 233 hectares.

cases.community: The project rehabilitated and upgraded the 7.6 km 33/11 kV distribution line from Blackhall Road to Wellington substation in east Freetown, replacing 54 towers, in what the Ministry of Energy's own plan calls a highly congested area holding the largest number of industries in Freetown. The abbreviated resettlement action plan of 29 April 2016 states that the work 'will result in permanent displacement impacts for local communities who live and/or own business units along the 7.6km stretch', that structures breaching the right of way or safety clearances 'require full or partial demolition', and that other dwellings would be hit temporarily by excavation, concrete work and the stringing of the lines. It identifies 107 project-affected persons, of whom 81 owned structures marked for partial demolition and 26 would have their structures completely demolished. The same plan records what happened the last time the line was cleared: the National Power Authority's 2010 resettlement plan identified 23 affected people, only 22 of the 23 were compensated for properties mapped for demolition, compensation was paid on condition that people demolished their own structures afterwards, 'However, not all the PAPs complied and have continued to occupy the RoW'. A further plan prepared in 2012 was never implemented. People who had been compensated in 2010 and had not demolished or moved were entitled this time only to movement and demolition assistance and livelihood support, not to cash for their structures. The cut-off date was 31 January 2015. The plan notes that over 75 per cent of the affected people did not depend on the land for a living and a similar share would suffer only partial demolition, and that an inter-ministerial sub-committee was formed, with the Strategy and Policy Unit in the office of the President overseeing the project, 'In anticipation of any potential resistance by the current occupants to prevent the project from taking place'; the plan adds that this was done to ensure the Government and the President achieved the agenda of providing electricity in Freetown, and concludes 'As a result the chances that resistance to relocate might arise is minimal if not none'. On the outcome, the completion report states that the dismantling and stringing of towers 'resulted in additional damage to properties', that the design followed the existing right of way from an earlier project's plans, that there was minimal buffer for work space, and that the client's safeguards specialist resigned and took time to replace. It records that safeguards preparation and compensation payments 'started of satisfactorily but deteriorated to Moderately Unsatisfactory in the last months to project closure', and that the plan 'was implemented satisfactorily with only two outstanding cash compensation (totaling about 1000 USD) largely attributed to procedural bottlenecks': one person had not been present when assets were enumerated and the other case involved several claimants in court. The unit paid additional compensation during implementation to people left out, to people whose further land was needed, and for inconvenience to one person caused by the project running long. Between 65 and 70 affected people took part in a livelihood restoration programme, all of them receiving seedlings for vegetable gardening, and 68 hand washing basins, hand sanitiser and soap were handed out during the Ebola crisis. The Independent Evaluation Group adds that during preparation, compensation was paid to 164 households for moving structures out of the right of way for safety, under the resettlement plan of the earlier Bank-financed Power and Water Project.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 888 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Ministry of Energy's abbreviated resettlement action plan of 29 April 2016 identifies 107 project-affected persons, 26 of whom were to have their structures completely demolished and 81 partially. No Bank document found gives a count of people actually relocated, and the completion report gives no figure for how many of the 107 were paid or moved.
cases.outcome: The grant closed on 31 July 2017, extended from 31 October 2015, to finish the Freetown upgrade and the resettlement plan that went with it. By the end of 2016 the Freetown upgrade and its compensation and relocation were the only activities still running. At the completion report's writing, one of the two outstanding compensation payments had been made and the court case over the other was unresolved; the Ministry responsible for energy said it expected to use interest earnings on project funds to pay it once the court decided, and the remaining issues were passed to a later Bank project, the Energy Sector Utility Reform Project. The contractor resolved all compensation for damage caused during construction. The Independent Evaluation Group's lesson on this project is that 'insufficient attention on the part of both the Bank and the borrower to oversee compliance with social and environmental safeguards undermined compliance of safeguards relating to involuntary resettlement during implementation'. The report rates safeguards compliance overall Moderately Satisfactory and records the project as in compliance with social and environmental safeguards at the time the report was finalised.

cases.community: The project rebuilt the Dili to Ainaro road in five lots. The resettlement impacts were concentrated on Lot 2, the Laulara to Solerema section. The project's updated resettlement plan for that lot, dated August 2018 and disclosed on 7 November 2018, counts 242 affected people or household heads with 1,454 household members on the old alignment, plus 11 people with 105 household members on the re-alignments. Of the 242, the plan's summary says twice that '26 APs with 146 households will be displaced since their residential structures need to be demolished to accommodate the design', while a later section of the same plan puts it at 12 affected persons with 84 households; the plan uses 'households' and 'family members' interchangeably throughout, and gives the household total as 1,454 in one place and 1,545 in another. A further 164 units of structures owned by 123 affected people were listed for demolition, of which 102 were temporary roadside stalls, called barakas, owned by 82 households; 13 permanent and 8 semi-permanent commercial structures were severely affected, along with 8 permanent, 4 semi-permanent and 8 temporary residential structures, 13 temporary kitchens, 7 permanent, 2 semi-permanent and 2 temporary toilets, 78.9 metres of concrete fence, 245 metres of temporary fence and 203 metres of cyclone wire. The residential structures severely affected on the old alignment came to 1,190.63 square metres, belonging to 34 affected people with 171 household members. The plan records that 'All the surveyed assets encroached on the land owned by the government' and that no private land had to be acquired, because the affected people occupied the government's 3 to 5 metre reserved strip. Its own view of the demolitions was that 'it is apparent that relocation is not a preference considering the available spaces for them to re-organize at the upper and/or lower portion of their present residence'. The plan also records 7,432 trees inventoried for removal along the old alignment, of which 5,364 were fruit or fruit-timber trees and 796 timber trees, and 2,847 trees already removed during the construction of re-alignments and bypasses, owned by 11 people. The outcome is in the completion report, which rates social safeguards compliance overall Satisfactory, with the Bank's safeguard requirements observed, and records that the resettlement plan for Lot 2, with its supplemental plan, 'was implemented completely with the compensation paid to all affected people (nevertheless, as noted in Aide Memoires, the execution of the Resettlement Plans for all road sections suffered delays)'. Payments on Lots 1, 3, 4 and 5 were finished except for a few cases where bank account details had to be corrected, and the total number of affected people across all five lots was 1,184, made up of 152 on Lot 1, 222 on Lot 2, 207 on Lot 3, 253 on Lot 4 and 350 on Lot 5. The report also records that 'Delay in resolving of Resettlement issues and civil grievances resulted in frequent stoppage of work by the contractor'. Fifty-three grievances were registered over the project, of which 43 were social, 6 were resettlement and 4 were environmental, health and safety matters. One incident of gender-based violence was reported and addressed by completion. A tree fell on a house in April 2022.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 851 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The completion report's own count of affected people across all five lots is 1,184, and it gives no count of anyone relocated. The nearest figure to a count of people moved is in the project's own updated resettlement plan for Lot 2 of August 2018, which states twice that 26 affected people with 146 households 'will be displaced since their residential structures need to be demolished', and once that the number is 12 affected people with 84 households. Those are plan figures in a plan that contradicts itself, and the plan's own view is that 'relocation is not a preference considering the available spaces for them to re-organize at the upper and/or lower portion of their present residence'. No document found counts anyone relocated, so the field is not filled.
cases.killed_note: The completion report records two fatal traffic incidents involving the project's workers, in August and September 2022, which 'were not reported immediately'; the Ministry of Public Works submitted root cause analysis reports for both on 23 November 2022, and the Bank then required the contractor's drivers and operators to be retrained by the supervision engineer, safety and speed limit signs and proper barricading to be installed, and a vehicle safety inspection report on all vehicles, all by 21 December 2022. Neither death is counted, because neither document states a cause for either. The report names one of them in its lessons section, where it says stone masonry guard rails 'should be improved upon or replaced with alternative materials with greater capacity to protect road users' and to retain occupants of faster or heavier vehicles 'as to avoid fatal incidents, such as the one involving a loader operator of the TLRCRP Lot 2 contractor - on August 14, 2022'; that is a recommendation about the project's guard rails, not a finding on what caused the death, and the contents of the root cause analyses are not given. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of this report records the four environmental, health and safety grievances but does not mention either fatality. Separately, the completion report notes that residents and road users raised safety concerns about the rebuilt road's higher speeds and traffic volumes and that more motorbike crashes have been seen, 'even though they reported not seeing or knowing of any fatal injuries, and most of the outcomes being minor injuries'.
cases.outcome: The last credit closed on 31 December 2022, seven years after the original closing date. The Lot 2 resettlement plan was recorded as implemented in full with compensation paid to all affected people, and social safeguards compliance was rated overall Satisfactory, after delays noted in mission reports on every lot and work stoppages the report attributes to unresolved resettlement issues and civil grievances. The completion report also records that a pre-construction road safety audit was commissioned for the whole corridor and for the Lot 1 design, with recommendations to be incorporated, and that these 'were not effectively implemented, nor the road safety approach fully embedded in the subsequent activities; it was a missed opportunity not making the corridor safe for every road user, especially around schools where more footpaths and traffic calming measures are needed'.

cases.community: The project rehabilitated and maintained federal roads across Nigeria. The completion report states that the rehabilitated roads were built within the existing right of way 'and therefore there was minimal relocation of PAPs. Nevertheless, a total of 675 PAPs had to relocate their businesses during construction works.' Site-specific abbreviated resettlement plans were prepared road by road and give the make-up of that figure. The plan for the Akure to Ilesha road, dated October 2012 with a cut-off of 18 November 2012, counts 130 people who own structures or trade within 10 metres of the carriageway centreline and lists the losses as loss of business premises, loss of income from business premises and loss of permanent structures, with an implementation cost of N7,294,407.13 plus a 10 per cent contingency. The plan for the Gombe to Biu road counts 190 people trading within 3.65 metres of the road edge, with losses of business premises and income but no loss of permanent structures, mostly people using tables or makeshift kiosks to sell palm oil, grains, beans, tea, bread, noodles, sugar cane and black-market petrol and engine oil, and notes women who sun-dry farm produce at the roadside as a vulnerable group to be given platforms elsewhere. The plan for the Mokwa to Bida road counts 366 people. The plan for the alternate bridge at km 7+350 on the Enugu to Abakaliki road lists among the things in the way a woman's local shop, naming her as Patricia Anyanwu, along with local sand miners, a block industry, pipelines and a perimeter fence, and about 8 metres by 100 metres of Otukwu village land with economic trees on it. On what happened, the completion report says that 'Largely the owners of these businesses have been compensated and all have confirmed their satisfaction, though payments were later than expected', and then records the specific failure: 'During the April 2016 Implementation Support Mission, it was observed that the Project Affected People along Akure-Ilesha road had not been paid compensation as late as March 2016, even though the works had been completed.' The reason given is that money for resettlement was not available, partly because of problems in adopting a single treasury account in 2012. Counterpart funds were later released and the report states that payment was then made to all affected people.
cases.displaced_label: 675 project-affected persons who 'had to relocate their businesses during construction works' - trading places, not dwellings (World Bank completion report, paragraph 73, 29 December 2017); the project's own road-by-road plans estimated 130 on Akure to Ilesha, 190 on Gombe to Biu and 366 on Mokwa to Bida
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 750 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The completion report's figure of 675 counts people who moved a business, not a home; it states that the roads were built inside the existing right of way and that relocation of affected people was minimal. The three road plans' own counts of 130, 190 and 366 are estimates made before the works for three of the five roads that had plans, and come to 686 between them; the completion report gives 675 for the project as a whole and no road-by-road outcome count, so the two sets of figures are not measuring the same thing.
cases.outcome: The credit closed on 30 June 2017. The completion report states that with every affected person compensated, compliance with the Bank's social safeguard policy was rated satisfactory, and that environmental compliance was initially weak but improved with additional oversight by Bank specialists. The project's own outcome was rated Moderately Unsatisfactory by both the completion report and the Independent Evaluation Group. The road fatality rate it was meant to cut from 161 to 120 deaths per 10,000 vehicles reached 143.

cases.confidence_note: The 675 people who moved their businesses, the unpaid compensation on the Akure to Ilesha road in March 2016 after the works were finished, and the reason given for it all come from the Bank's own completion report; the Independent Evaluation Group's review of that report repeats them. The road-by-road counts come from the Federal Ministry of Works' own resettlement plans, which are plans and not records of what was done. No independent account of these roadside traders was found; one academic study of traders displaced by road widening in Akure covers the Arakale road, a different, state-financed project of 2010 to 2011. No document found says how many people on the Akure to Ilesha road were unpaid, how long they waited, what any of them received, or whether the women who sun-dried produce beside the Gombe to Biu road were ever given the platforms the plan promised. The completion report also states that all the business owners 'have confirmed their satisfaction' and that payment was eventually made to all of them.
cases.conditions: A resettlement policy framework was prepared and disclosed before appraisal. The Independent Evaluation Group's review records that 'The project was not expected to result in loss of land. However, a Resettlement Policy Framework (RPF) was prepared in case relocation of' people proved necessary, with a detailed resettlement plan to follow the detailed design of each road. Site-specific abbreviated plans were then prepared and disclosed for the Akure to Ilesha, Gombe to Biu, Mokwa to Bida, Enugu to Abakaliki and Ogoja to Ikom roads in 2010 and 2012, with environmental management plans for the periodically maintained roads. The 2 February 2011 restructuring changed the project's legal covenants. The report gives the non-availability of funds for resettlement, partly from the adoption of a single treasury account by the federal government in 2012, as the reason compensation went unpaid after works were complete (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 29 December 2017; IEG ICR Review ICRR0021110).
