lenders.name: Global Environment Facility, through the World Bank
lenders.role: Grant TF-53110 of US$5.5 million for the Greater Addo Elephant National Park Project (P064438). Approved 24 February 2004, effective 28 June 2004 against an original date of 30 April 2004, mid-term review 21 May 2007. The revised amount and the amount disbursed were both US$5.3 million. Original closing was 30 April 2010; actual closing was 30 October 2010 after a six-month extension requested in 2009. Environmental category B and global focal area B. The project triggered three safeguard policies, environmental assessment, physical cultural resources and involuntary resettlement. The implementing agency was South African National Parks. The Bank was responsible for approving the resettlement action plan. The completion report of 27 April 2011 rated outcome Satisfactory, risk to the global environment outcome Low or Negligible, Bank performance Satisfactory and borrower performance Highly Satisfactory; the Independent Evaluation Group's review ICRR13655, posted 7 November 2013, rated outcome Moderately Satisfactory and risk to development outcome Moderate. The mid-term review cut the target for terrestrial area under park management from 236,000 to 205,000 hectares and for private land under contractual arrangement from 46,000 to 30,000 hectares, and the grant agreement was amended to match (Implementation Completion and Results Report ICR00001883, 27 April 2011; IEG ICR Review ICRR13655, 7 November 2013).

companies.name: South African National Parks
companies.role: The statutory national parks agency of South Africa and the project's implementing agency, which bought the farms, prepared and ran the resettlement policy framework and resettlement action plan, and chaired the quarterly Resettlement Working Group. It also commissioned the independent audit of the plan's implementation in 2010 and provided the resettled people with jobs in the park's management programmes or grants under the project's small, medium and micro-enterprise scheme (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 27 April 2011).

cases.community: The project paid for the expansion of the Addo Elephant National Park by buying farms from willing sellers in the Sundays River Valley. The resettlement action plan of 17 June 2003 sets out whose homes those farms were. It records that during phase 1, for 13 farms, 'it is estimated that 165 workers and an additional 544 dependants will fall within the ambit of the RPF', and that on the 6 priority farms surveyed there were 35 farm workers and 34 dependants, 69 inhabitants in all, averaging 3.3 people and 1.7 workers to a household. It describes the people: 84 per cent aged 18 to 49, 73 per cent men, 24 per cent with no education at all and only 13 per cent with any secondary schooling, 63 per cent having worked only on farms, median income R588 a month. It records that a large part of their income came in kind - meat, staple foods, water, limited electricity, firewood, housing, clothing, limited transport, loans and the right to keep livestock on the farm - benefits that did not stop at retirement, so that 'the elderly have a safety net provided by the farmer. Once displaced from the farn, such benefits would fall away.' The plan answers its own concern, undertaking that South African National Parks 'will ensure that incomes are replaced via the income restoration strategy outlined in this document'. It states the concern plainly: 'concern has been expressed that farm workers would be likely to lose access to employment and places of accommodation typically provided on the farms. Farm workers are regarded as among the most vulnerable members of South Africa's working class'. The outcome, in the completion report, is that the plan and its socio-economic programme were prepared 'to resettle 29 households or Project Affected Persons (PAP) in two surrounding municipalities (Sundays River Valley and Blue Crane) and to help the displaced individuals to recover their overall livelihoods', and that of those 29, 'A group of 11 households were moved to municipal houses, another group of 10 households were moved to houses provided by SANParks and a last group of 8 households have not been moved.' On the eight, the Bank's social safeguards specialist visited the municipal government and was shown a council resolution letter putting all of them on the Reconstruction and Development Programme housing list on a priority basis, with houses to be built on their plots when each municipality's next housing project started. 'One RAP individual is not on the (RDP) housing list for Blue Crane Municipality and has chosen not to respond to assistance offers by RDP.' On the 21 who had moved, the report states that the Bank's social safeguards specialist visited the new houses 'and was satisfied with these arrangements as all the affected households were in better housing conditions than before the move'. Everyone affected was given either a job in one of the park's management programmes or a grant under the project's small, medium and micro-enterprise scheme. Teresa Connor's field study of the same park expansion, published in Development Southern Africa in 2005, records the mechanism: the park 'has subsequently been purchasing properties on a “willing seller/willing buyer” basis, which requires that a farm be cleared of all previous inhabitants upon transfer to a new owner', and notes the loss of small stock farms to conservation enterprises 'of which the GAENP is the major player'.
cases.displaced_label: 11 households moved into municipal houses and 10 into houses provided by South African National Parks, with 8 of the 29 households the plan covered not moved by the project's close (World Bank completion report, 27 April 2011). No document prints a total of those moved, so none is given here.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 709 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The completion report records that the resettlement action plan was written for 29 households, that 11 were moved into municipal houses, 10 into houses provided by South African National Parks and that 'a last group of 8 households have not been moved'. The Independent Evaluation Group's review opens with '29 households were resettled' and then gives the same three groups, saying the 8 'are scheduled to move to housing projects but are waiting for relocation', so the two documents record the same outcome in different words. The project's own resettlement action plan of 2003 estimated that 165 workers and 544 dependants on 13 farms would fall within the resettlement policy framework in phase 1 alone, against the 29 households the plan was eventually written for.
cases.outcome: The grant closed on 30 October 2010. Of the 29 households, 11 had moved into municipal houses and 10 into houses South African National Parks provided, and the Bank's social safeguards specialist recorded all of them as better housed than before. Eight were still waiting, on a municipal housing list, for houses to be built when the next housing projects began, and one person was not on the list at all. An independent audit of the resettlement plan's implementation, ordered early in 2010, concluded that South African National Parks had met its obligations to the 29, and the Bank's last social safeguards supervision mission, in May 2010, agreed. The park's terrestrial area reached 170,115 hectares against a revised target of 205,000, and 17,608 hectares of private land were brought in under contractual arrangement against a revised target of 30,000, because land prices rose from between R1,080 and R1,315 a hectare in 2003 and 2004 to between R7,000 and R8,817 a hectare by 2010 and some owners would not sell. An 11,000-hectare conservation agreement with the Enon Bersheba community did not happen, because the state had not transferred the title to the community.

cases.confidence_note: The 29 households, the split into 11, 10 and 8, the one person off the housing list and the finding that those who moved were better housed than before all come from the Bank's own completion report, and the Independent Evaluation Group's review repeats them. That is the lender reporting on its own project, and nothing outside the Bank reports on these 29 households. The description of the farm workers and the loss of their in-kind income comes from South African National Parks' own resettlement action plan of 2003, which is a plan and which undertakes that their incomes would be replaced. Teresa Connor's field study of the same park expansion, in Development Southern Africa in 2005, corroborates the mechanism - the park 'has subsequently been purchasing properties on a “willing seller/willing buyer” basis, which requires that a farm be cleared of all previous inhabitants upon transfer to a new owner' - but gives no count of farms or workers displaced and does not report on the households the Bank's plan covered. No document found names any of the 29 households, says when they moved, says what they were paid, or says whether the eight households still waiting in 2010 ever got houses. The independent audit of the resettlement plan that the completion report relies on, by South African National Parks in 2010, is listed as unpublished and was not found. The completion report's cover is dated 27 April 2011 and its own data sheet gives the report date as 28 April 2011.
cases.conditions: The project triggered environmental assessment, physical cultural resources and involuntary resettlement. A resettlement policy framework was completed during preparation in 2003 and a resettlement action plan followed on 17 June 2003, with an abbreviated resettlement plan in 2006; the Bank was responsible for approving the plan. A Resettlement Working Group met quarterly to monitor the policy's application and its minutes are available. South African National Parks set aside enough of its own budget to cover all the costs the plan anticipated. South African legislation, the Bank's physical cultural resources policy and the agency's own heritage policies produced a Cultural Resource Framework in 2003 with a detailed inventory of cultural resources. South Africa's Extension of Security of Tenure Act and Land Reform (Labour Tenants) Act protect farm dwellers' and labour tenants' security of tenure and are cited in the resettlement plan's legal section (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 27 April 2011; Resettlement Action Plan, 17 June 2003).
